title: Chatbots Have a Math Problem and a People Problem
author: Dan Meyer
summary: Dan Meyer shares the prepared remarks he gave to a working group of education funders considering how much money to direct toward generative-AI projects, positioning himself between AI optimists and pessimists with the deliberately understated claim that chatbots are simply "neat." He argues chatbots have a math problem: students communicate new mathematical understanding through gestures, sketches, and half-formed talk, and translating that informal thinking into text for a chatbot -- and translating the chatbot's formal reply back into their own understanding -- imposes a cognitive tax students pay alone, unlike classroom activities such as Amplify's Function Carnival that directly invite noticings and sketches. He also argues chatbots have a people problem, tracing the "chatbot theory of learning" back to personalized-learning models that treat classmates as liabilities to be segregated from rather than assets to learn with, and citing a Gates-funded RAND study that found personalized learning produced no significant reading gains and only modest math gains, while decreasing students' sense of belonging. Meyer contrasts this with a live classroom example of a teacher using two students' differing graphs to generate a moment of collective mathematical insight that a chatbot-mediated, individualized model cannot replicate. He closes arguing that math students are trying to "figure out math and figure out themselves at the same time" against a difficult social and economic backdrop, and that a chatbot is not equal to that assignment.
points: Meyer's "math problem": chatbots only understand a single formal, textual dialect, forcing students to translate their informal gestures, sketches, and half-formed thinking into text and back -- a cognitive tax paid alone.

Meyer's "people problem": the chatbot theory of learning inherits personalized learning's premise that classmates are liabilities to segregate from, when a Gates-funded RAND study found that framing decreased students' sense of belonging.
The same RAND study found no significant reading gains and only modest math gains from personalized learning, while classroom discussion carries an effect size, via Hattie, many times larger.

Meyer contrasts chatbot-mediated individualized learning with a live example of a teacher using two students' differing graphs to generate collective insight -- something he argues the chatbot model cannot replicate.
quotes: Whereas I predict some modest quality-of-life improvements for teachers and students over the next five years, Khan has claimed that AI tools like his Khanmigo represent "the biggest positive transformation that education has ever seen.
That translation process represents a cognitive tax, one which students pay coming and going, one which they pay alone.
Personalized learning declares that these students are liabilities to each other, rather than assets.

RAND found the result of telling students that they and their classmates are liabilities to each other, rather than assets, was a decrease in feelings of belonging and community in the personalized learning condition (p. 24).
Chatbots are neat, but in K-12 math education, they are not much more than that.
